correctness.rationale: A complete orthonormal spin-three/spin-one basis for the four-dimensional real two-coordinate third Wiener chaos is verified. Exact polar-moment integration establishes \(\mathbb E F^4=30a^4+168a^2b^2+66b^4+40\sqrt3\,ab^3\cos\delta\). The stability remainder reduces to the least eigenvalue \(72-8\sqrt{39}\) of the symmetric matrix \(\begin{psmallmatrix}108&-20\sqrt3\\-20\sqrt3&36\end{psmallmatrix}\), with exact nontrivial equality eigenvector; the upper deficit factorizes into nonnegative factors and is attained precisely by one-coordinate third Hermite polynomials. An independently computed exact 35-coefficient fourth-moment expansion is checked from the embedded script; endpoints and zero-component cases are treated. No finite test is used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Checked primary work gives fourth-moment convergence/contraction criteria (Nualart–Peccati 2005), cumulant moderate-deviation bounds (Schulte–Thäle 2014), and product-square chaos lower inequalities (Malicet–Nourdin–Peccati–Poly 2015). These do not imply the explicit global sharp mixed binary-cubic lower bound and optimal transverse eigenvalue remainder. A prior exact homogeneous cubic spherical-harmonic theorem explains the value 30 on the harmonic restriction only, and the rank-one upper endpoint has classical antecedents. An exact equivalent binary Wick-cubic computation in unindexed literature remains a real residual risk.
residual_risks: The exact binary third-chaos quartic invariant and stability eigenvalue might be a corollary recorded in an unindexed older monograph or invariant-theory treatment.

value.rationale: The first two-coordinate third-order Gaussian chaos already separates harmonic and trace-type irreducible components. An exact global \(L^4/L^2\) lower inequality plus best sharp transverse defect constant quantifies this structural decomposition and classifies all zero, rank-one and mixed equality modes. It is a natural fixed-dimension norm-geometry problem motivated by fourth-moment theory, not an arbitrary finite lookup or a single textbook Hermite moment.
